title: Kama burned to ash, and not gone
hookLine: Shiva burns the god of love to ash, yet love stays one of life's rightful aims.
carry: kama is a rightful aim, in its fitting place
tomorrow: a powerful man wants what isn't his. which aim should have won?

lines: A FLOWER ARROW AT A YOGI.
cards: The gods need Shiva to marry Parvati, but Shiva sits deep in meditation, wanting nothing. So they send Kama, the god of love, with his bow of sugarcane and his arrows of flowers. Spring arrives out of season.
Kama takes aim at the yogi. Shiva's third eye opens, and fire turns Kama to ash. His wife Rati weeps over the ashes.
Yet love doesn't leave the world. In the tellings Kama lives on without a body, as Ananga, the bodiless one, and Parvati wins Shiva in the end by her own devotion and discipline.

teach.b: Hindu teaching doesn't do what Shiva's fire seems to do. It doesn't abolish desire. It names kama, joy and love, as one of the aims of a human life, beside dharma, artha and moksha.
The Kama Sutra is well-known for one thing, and its frank chapters for adults stay on the shelf here. But it opens with a chapter that reads like philosophy.
Vatsyayana, the author it names, defines each aim. Dharma is doing what scripture asks and holding back from what it forbids.
Artha is gaining what's worth having, learning, land, goods, and friends, then protecting it and helping it grow.

teach.h: FITTING JOY OF THE FIVE SENSES.
teach.b: And kama is the enjoyment of fitting things by the five senses, with the mind and the self taking part. Two words carry the weight.

Fitting: pleasure that suits, not just any appetite; many readers add, suited to the moment too. One way to read Kama's ash with this chapter in hand: his arrow flew at the wrong moment, at a yogi deep in meditation.

teach.h: WITH THE MIND AND SELF THERE.
teach.b: And the mind and the self: pleasure with someone actually there for it. Earlier on this path, the Gita called kama a smoke that clouds what we know.

teach.h: A RIGHTFUL AIM, IN ITS FITTING PLACE.
teach.b: Here the same word names a rightful aim, with limits. The tradition holds both.

how: Kama, the god of love, is pictured with a sugarcane bow and flower arrows; his burning by Shiva is told in the Puranas and in Kalidasa's poem Kumarasambhava. Scholars of Hindu ethics read the Kama Sutra's opening chapters beside the dharma texts, because they define dharma, artha and kama.

games.q: what does “the kama sutra's ethics chapter” mean?
o: the part of a well-known old book that tells a love story
the part of a well-known old book that lists a king's laws
the part of a well-known old book that weighs a whole life's aims

games.q: three aims, defined — tap the pairs.
p: learned from scripture and those who know it
fitting joy of the five senses
Kama, living on without a body

s: after Shiva burned Kama, Hindu teaching treats all desire as an enemy to wipe out
kama stays one of the aims of life; Kama lives on bodiless, and Shiva marries Parvati in the end.
its definition of artha includes friends
learning, land, gold, cattle, goods, and friends, gained, protected and grown.
the chapter defines kama as any appetite at all
it says fitting things, enjoyed by the senses with the mind and the self taking part.

games.q: you're eating lunch at your desk while answering emails, scrolling, and half-listening to a podcast. by the chapter's definition of kama, what's missing?
o: more at once. stacking pleasures is more kama.
the mind and the self, actually present for one fitting pleasure.
nothing. kama is just the senses being busy.
games.why: the chapter defines kama as fitting things enjoyed by the senses with the mind and the self taking part. busy senses aren't the same as being there.

practice: If there's something near you with a smell, tea, soap, an orange peel, bring it close and breathe it in slowly. Stay with that one smell for the whole sit, your whole attention there.
If you pray, end with a quiet thank you, the way many Hindus offer food before they eat. If you don't, simply notice it fully.

wordCard.voice: The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter: where kama is defined as fitting joy of the five senses, with the mind and the self there too.

orig.note: Sanskrit kama: desire, pleasure, love; here, one of the three aims of life.

carryVoice: Your line: kama is a rightful aim, in its fitting place. Shiva's fire didn't end love. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Kalidasa, Kumarasambhava, cantos 3–5 (Kama's arrow at Shiva in meditation; Shiva's third eye burns him; Rati's grief; Parvati wins Shiva by tapas); the burning of Kama is also told in the Puranas
Kama Sutra 1.2 (definitions of dharma, artha and kama; where each is learned)
Bhagavad Gita 3.37–3.39 (kama as the enemy, covering knowledge like smoke over fire)
